summary: Generalizes the technique of using a packet's TTL or hop limit to check that it came from a directly connected neighbor. Packets that arrive with a lower value than expected are rejected. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 3682 and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Letters from your next-door neighbor arrive with a fresh stamp. If a stamp looks old, it came from far away and gets thrown out. That is a simple way to block distant attackers.

questions: why does gtsm drop packets with low ttl
subtitle: Send routing-protocol packets with TTL 255 and drop anything that arrives with less, so distant attackers cannot pose as a neighbor.

tldr.problem: A router's control plane can be flooded with forged protocol packets from outside the network, using up its CPU and other scarce resources.
tldr.mechanism: Peers send protocol packets with the TTL (IPv4) or Hop Limit (IPv6) set to 255. The receiver classifies packets by whether the TTL matches what an adjacent peer would produce, and can drop the ones that do not.
tldr.outcome: It is a cheap defense against remote attackers on single-hop sessions. It obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3682 and puts the mechanism on the Standards Track, but it is not a substitute for authentication.

facts.label: Default state when added to a protocol
facts.value: Not enabled (SHOULD NOT be on by default)

today: RFC 5082 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaces the Experimental RFC 3682.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) protects a router's IP-based control plane from attacks that burn CPU. Cryptography can protect infrastructure such as BGP against many attacks, but many CPU-overload attacks can be stopped by this much simpler check.

It rests on one observation: most protocol peerings are between adjacent routers, either directly connected interfaces or, in the worst case, loopback to loopback with static routes. Since TTL spoofing is considered nearly impossible, an expected TTL value gives a simple and reasonably robust defense against forged packets from outside the network.

The RFC is clear about the limit: GTSM is not a substitute for authentication and does not secure against insider on-the-wire attacks such as spoofing or replay. TTL and Hop Limit have identical semantics for GTSM, so the document just says "TTL" for both.
sections.eli5: Routers mostly talk to the router right next to them. So a message that has traveled a long way is suspicious, and a simple check can spot it.

sections.title: Assumptions Underlying GTSM
sections.content:
GTSM works under five assumptions: most peerings are between adjacent routers; providers may or may not use strict ingress filtering on non-trusted links; use is OPTIONAL and can be configured per peer (group); both peers implement it; and the router can put differently classified traffic into separate resource pools, such as queues or processing quotas.

The DoS protection only works if packets are classified and separated before they reach a scarce resource. The closer GTSM runs to line-rate hardware, the more resistant the system is. The RFC does not say how to separate resources, nor what else a router may do with non-matching packets.

Attackers are assumed able to send control traffic that looks valid, with the source and destination of configured peers. Every router on the path is assumed to decrement TTL properly. Tunnels are assumed not to be a back door for TTL spoofing: there are no tunneled packets terminating on the router, or the tunnels are secure with trusted endpoints, or decapsulation prevents source spoofing, or the session does not accept packets from a tunnel.

With existing protocols, GTSM is configured manually. No automatic negotiation is defined. A new protocol with built-in support is recommended to always use it; if dynamic negotiation is needed, the negotiation messages MUST be authenticated by other means.
sections.eli5: The trick only works if you only trust your neighbors, if the post office stamps every letter honestly, and if you sort suspicious letters away before they clog your desk.

sections.title: The GTSM Procedure
sections.content:
If GTSM is an add-on to an existing protocol (the RFC names BGP, LDP and MSDP), it SHOULD NOT be enabled by default, to stay backward-compatible. A protocol with built-in dynamic negotiation MAY suggest GTSM, but it is enabled only if both peers agree.

Sending: the TTL of every IP packet belonging to a GTSM-enabled session MUST be set to 255. This includes related ICMP error messages. Where the forwarding plane would decrement the TTL of control-plane traffic, the TTL of GTSM sessions MUST NOT be decremented.

Receiving: each packet addressed to the control plane is put into one of three categories: Unknown (not tied to any GTSM-enabled session), Trusted (tied to a session, TTL in the expected range) or Dangerous (tied to a session, TTL not in the expected range).

The exact policy per category is configurable, but by default implementations SHOULD keep Dangerous packets from competing for resources with Trusted or Unknown ones, MUST NOT drop Trusted or Unknown packets as part of GTSM processing, and MAY drop Dangerous packets.
sections.eli5: Every message from a neighbor gets the freshest stamp, 255. Messages with that stamp go in the good pile, messages with a worn stamp go in the suspicious pile, and strangers' mail goes in a third pile.

sections.title: Why TTL 255 Is Hard to Spoof
sections.content:
A TTL of 255 is non-trivial to spoof because each router on the path decrements it by one. A receiver may not be able to tell whether a source address is valid, but it can tell how many router hops away the packet came from. Engineering a 255 from a non-directly connected location is not possible, assuming the neighbors are not compromised, the packet was not tunneled to the decapsulator, and routers follow RFC 791.

Tunnels are the main exception. If a tunnel is not integrity-protected, the lower layer is compromised. When the tunnel ends at the protocol peer, the peer sees whatever inner TTL the sender chose, so security depends on the tunnel. When the tunnel tail-end instead forwards to a directly connected peer, normal IP forwarding decrements the TTL, so a legitimate packet cannot arrive with 255. The RFC walks through IP-in-IP (RFC 2003), GRE (RFC 2784) and MPLS (RFC 3443).

For MPLS, GTSM checks are possible over Pipe model LSPs but not over Uniform model LSPs, where the ingress TTL for a multi-hop LSP will be 254 or less and the check fails.

Other limits: an attacker directly connected to an interface can disturb a GTSM-protected session unless ingress filtering is applied, so unfiltered interfaces must be trusted. GTSM also will not protect against attackers as close as the legitimate peer.
sections.eli5: Every router a letter passes through wears a little off the stamp, so nobody far away can show up with a perfectly fresh one. Secret tunnels are the exception, because they can hide how far a letter really went.

sections.title: Fragments and Multi-Hop Sessions
sections.content:
Non-initial IP fragments carry no transport-layer information, so they likely cannot be tied to a GTSM session and are classified Unknown. A legitimate first fragment can then be combined with spoofed later fragments unless the implementation remembers and checks the TTL of every fragment. If it does check and one fails, the reassembled packet is Dangerous.

Reassembly also weakens the assumption that packets are classified before reaching a scarce resource. So operators may need to rate-limit or discard all fragments, and it is highly RECOMMENDED that GTSM-protected protocols avoid fragmentation, for example by manual MTU tuning or Path MTU Discovery.

Multi-hop sessions are not specified. Appendix A, which is non-normative, says a receiver could check that the TTL is within a configured number of hops from 255, for example accepting 254 or 255, but this has different security implications and needs experimentation. The RFC notes that GTSM might fit multi-hop cases with a fairly static, well-known topology and a trusted network between the peers.
sections.eli5: If a letter is cut into pieces, only the first piece shows the stamp, so it is hard to be sure the rest are real. It is best not to cut letters up at all.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3682
sections.content:
RFC 5082 obsoletes RFC 3682, which was Experimental. This one is on the Standards Track.

The listed changes: new text on applicability and use in new and existing protocols, a narrower scope that leaves out multi-hop scenarios, an explicit requirement that related messages (ICMP errors) also be sent and checked at TTL 255, clarifications on fragmentation, tunneling and ingress filtering, and many editorial improvements.

The ICMP change can matter for compatibility. Some RFC 3682 implementations originate packets with TTL 255, but others use 64 or other values, and their related messages would be classified Dangerous. The RFC does not consider this a significant problem, because protocols do not depend on related messages and delivery of them is unreliable. It says that since ICMP errors are a significant attack vector, for example to reset sessions, the stricter rule seems sensible.
sections.eli5: This is the grown-up version of an earlier trial rule. It now also says that the small warning notes must carry the fresh stamp too.

items.label: No GTSM session
items.desc: Cannot be tied to any registered GTSM-enabled session. Must not be dropped by GTSM.

items.label: Session, TTL in range
items.desc: Belongs to a GTSM-enabled session and the TTL is in the expected range. Must not be dropped by GTSM.

items.label: Session, TTL out of range
items.desc: Belongs to a GTSM-enabled session but the TTL is not in the expected range. May be dropped.
